Targeting / Description: Pre-execution ML scoring, signature-less detection, polymorphic malware blocking before detonation
Parent Domain: Endpoint protection & response: Core EDR — agents on every managed device
Coverage Details: Real-time prevention and pre-execution ML scoring are architectural capabilities that require a dedicated NGAV/EDR agent on the endpoint. Our detection engine operates post-execution on telemetry and cannot perform this point-in-time stateless prevention.
Can we build it?: No. Relies on endpoint AV/EDR engine.

Targeting / Description: Continuous process telemetry, MITRE ATT&CK-mapped rules, real-time blocking of anomalous behaviour chains
Parent Domain: Endpoint protection & response: Core EDR — agents on every managed device
Coverage Details: Strong behavioral detection capability through stateful streaming correlation is fully covered by 470+ active correlation rules (e.g., AN0827-T1561.002-DET0297, AN0602-T1486-DET0215). Real-time prevention/blocking is out of scope as it requires an EDR agent. Assuming a SOAR platform is deployed, the SIEM detects/correlates the condition, and a SOAR playbook executes take response action via EDR API. (Conditional on integration being built and tested).
Can we build it?: Yes, via SOAR playbook calling EDR API.
Extra Tooling / Log Source Needed: SOAR playbook: take-response-action via EDR API

Targeting / Description: AMSI integration, reflective DLL injection detection, process hollowing, living-off-the land (LOLBAS) blocking
Parent Domain: Endpoint protection & response: Core EDR — agents on every managed device
Coverage Details: Process Hollowing detection is covered (rule AN1076-T1055.012-DET0382). However, we have significant gaps for the other techniques: To detect LOLBAS (hackers abusing built-in Windows tools), we need Sysmon Event ID 1 to see the exact tool name (OriginalFileName) and what command was typed (CommandLine). To detect hidden scripts via AMSI, we need Windows Event 1116/1117 to read the actual script content (ScriptBlockText). For Windows to even generate these logs, IT must first enable 'Script Block Logging' via Group Policy (GPO). Finally, detecting Reflective DLL (which hides directly in RAM) and real-time blocking are out of scope. SIEM only reads logs; scanning RAM and blocking attacks requires a dedicated EDR agent. Once detection is closed (via missing log), response is separately solvable via SOAR playbook + EDR, once integrated.
MITRE Technique: T1055 (Process Hollowing), T1620 (Reflective Code Loading), T1562.001 / T1059.001 (AMSI Bypass)
Can we build it?: Yes. AMSI rules can be built via logs and process creation patterns. Reflective loading can be built via Sysmon, but note: this is heuristic and prone to FPs.

Coverage Details: While we can audit when a hacker tampers with a host firewall, performing actual one-click network containment and remote site isolation are active response capabilities. Targeting / Description: CFG, DEP, ASLR enforcement; heap spray detection; stack pivot and ROP chain blocking; kernel exploit prevention
Parent Domain: Endpoint protection & response: Core EDR — agents on every managed device
Coverage Details: Enforcing memory protections (like ASLR/DEP) and actively blocking ROP chains or kernel exploits are OS-level mitigations. This requires tools like Windows Exploit Guard or an EDR's exploit mitigation module. A SIEM cannot physically enforce memory protections or block exploits in real-time.
Can we build it?: No. Exploit mitigation requires OS-level configuration.

Targeting / Description: PowerShell, WScript, Bash, Python, VBA, macro analysis — AMSI hooks at runtime, obfuscation deobfuscation engine
Parent Domain: Endpoint protection & response: Core EDR — agents on every managed device
Coverage Details: Basic script obfuscation checks (like hackers hiding commands with caret ^ symbols) are strongly covered by over 100 rules (e.g., AN1501-T1055.013-DET0544). However, our major gap is runtime deobfuscation. To catch advanced scripts that hide themselves, we desperately need Windows Event ID 1116/1117 (AMSI logs). This specific log gives us the clean, readable script content (ScriptBlockText) right before it executes. Without IT turning on 'Script Block Logging' via Group Policy (GPO), the SIEM is completely blind to advanced fileless scripts. Once detection is closed (via missing log), response is separately solvable via SOAR playbook + EDR, once integrated.
Can we build it?: Yes, but we need AMSI logs enabled on endpoints.

Targeting / Description: Per-device allow/block/read-only, vendor/serial granularity, audit trail, remote exception workflow, encrypted USB enforcement

Coverage Details: Detecting data being copied to USB drives via command-line heuristics is covered by rules AN0616-T1052.001-DET0220 and AN0342-T1052-DET0123. However, we have a gap in deterministic hardware auditing; to reliably log physical USB insertions, we need Windows Event ID 2003 (DriverFrameworks-UserMode) enabled. A SIEM cannot physically block hardware from mounting; this requires a dedicated EDR or DLP device control agent. Once detection is closed (via missing log), response is separately solvable via SOAR playbook + EDR, once integrated.
Can we build it?: Yes. Can build rules targeting actual USB insertion and block events.

Targeting / Description: Local ML models, cached policy, queued actions execute on reconnect — full protection during VPN/internet outage
Parent Domain: Endpoint protection & response: Core EDR — agents on every managed device
Coverage Details: Providing protection while an endpoint is completely offline requires an agent running locally on the machine with its own built-in ML models and cached policies. Because a SIEM relies 100% on centralized log forwarding over the network, it is physically impossible for the correlation engine to analyze events or protect a machine during an internet outage. This is a fundamental architectural requirement for a local EDR agent.

Targeting / Description: Full process tree, file create/modify/delete, network socket, registry change — 30–90 day searchable history
Parent Domain: Endpoint protection & response: Core EDR — agents on every managed device

Targeting / Description: Lightweight kernel sensor for servers, workload-aware tuning, container/VM visibility, privileged process monitoring

Coverage Details: Privileged process monitoring on Windows servers (like IIS and SQL) is strongly covered by over 30 rules (e.g., AN0219-T1190-DET0080). For container visibility, we need logs from tools like Falco or Kubernetes audit logs. Without these specific log sources forwarding to the SIEM, we are completely blind to Linux and container compromises. Once detection is closed (via missing log), response is separately solvable via SOAR playbook + EDR, once integrated.
Can we build it?: We can build Linux rules, but we need the telemetry and sensor deployment.

Targeting / Description: LSASS access monitoring, mimikatz/DCSync/pass-the-hash/pass-the-ticket detection, NTLM relay blocking
Parent Domain: Identity protection & privilege control: Credential, access, and escalation defence
Coverage Details: Detecting attempts to read LSASS memory (e.g., Mimikatz dumping passwords) is strongly covered by over 20 rules (e.g., AN0235-T1003.002-DET0085). A SIEM cannot enforce OS-level memory protections like Credential Guard or physically block network authentication relays. Once detection is closed (via missing log), response is separately solvable via SOAR playbook + EDR, once integrated.
Can we build it?: Yes for DCSync, but MUST filter Event 4662 on replication GUIDs (1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2, etc.) or it's too noisy. NTLM relay requires specific tools, not just logs.

Targeting / Description: Token impersonation, UAC bypass, sudo abuse, SeDebugPrivilege misuse, scheduled task privilege abuse alerts
Parent Domain: Identity protection & privilege control: Credential, access, and escalation defence
Coverage Details: Detecting Windows privilege escalation techniques like Token Impersonation, UAC Bypass, and Scheduled Task abuse is fully covered (via rules AN1324-T1134.001-DET0482, AN0786-T1134-DET0283, and AN0975-T1548-DET0345). However, we have specific log gaps for the remaining techniques: To deterministically catch SeDebugPrivilege misuse, we need Windows Event ID 4703 (Token Right Adjusted) enabled in advanced audit policy. To detect Linux sudo abuse, we need native Linux telemetry like Auditd or auth.log forwarded to the SIEM.
MITRE Technique: T1134 (Token Manipulation), T1548.002 (Bypass UAC), T1053.005 (Scheduled Task)
Can we build it?: Yes. Can build rules for Event 4703 (Token Right Adjusted) and Linux auditd logs.

Targeting / Description: AD/Entra anomaly detection, golden/silver ticket attacks, Kerberoasting, brute force, impossible travel alerts
Parent Domain: Identity protection & privilege control: Credential, access, and escalation defence
Coverage Details: Detecting on-premise Active Directory threats like Golden Tickets and Kerberoasting is fully covered by our existing rules (e.g., AN0405-T1558.001-DET0144). Coverage Details: Detecting suspicious admin account logins and lateral movement is strongly covered by over 50 rules (e.g., AN8015-T1021-DET8015, AN0327-T1210-DET0118). However, enforcing Just-In-Time (JIT) privileges and performing privileged session recording are out of scope. A SIEM can audit when admins log in, but managing their temporary access or actively recording their screen sessions requires a dedicated PAM platform (like CyberArk or BeyondTrust).

Targeting / Description: Non-human identity (API keys, service accounts, tokens) anomaly detection, over privileged account alerts

Coverage Details: Monitoring local Windows service accounts (like NETWORK SERVICE or SYSTEM) for anomalous behavior is fully covered by our existing rules (e.g., AN0786-T1134-DET0283). To detect abuse of cloud API keys or over-privileged service principals, we absolutely need cloud control plane logs like AWS CloudTrail, Azure Activity Logs, and Entra ID Service Principal sign-ins. Without these specific logs, our cloud service account visibility is zero.
Can we build it?: We need Cloud logs for API/NHI anomaly detection.

Targeting / Description: DNS tunnelling, DGA domain detection, HTTPS C2 decryption, periodic beacon pattern analysis, encrypted C2 over TOR/CDN
Parent Domain: Network detection & XDR correlation: Cross-source signal fusion, east-west, C2
Coverage Details: Behavioral beacon detection and periodic communication analysis using Zeek, Suricata, and endpoint telemetry are fully covered by over 20 correlation rules (e.g., AN8002-T1071-DET8002, AN0637-T1104-DET0228). A SIEM cannot decrypt live network traffic or perform deep packet inspection. This requires a dedicated Network Detection and Response (NDR) platform.

Targeting / Description: SMB/WMI/RDP anomaly, pass-the-hash spread, network share enumeration, service installation across hosts

Coverage Details: Detecting lateral movement across the network—including WMI anomalies, Pass-the-Hash spreads, SMB admin share enumeration, and remote service installations (Event ID 7045)—is fully covered. This represents a core strength of our SIEM correlation engine, with over 60 active rules successfully mapping to these specific techniques (e.g., AN0147-T1534-DET0054, AN0327-T1210-DET0118). No log source or architectural capability gaps exist for these detections.
Can we build it?: Yes, logic exists.

Targeting / Description: East-west traffic baselining, protocol anomaly, data exfiltration detection, IoT/OT/unmanaged host visibility

Coverage Details: Detecting data exfiltration and protocol anomalies using Zeek, Suricata, and network flow logs is fully covered by our existing correlation rules (e.g., AN0436-T1567.004-DET0153, AN1511-T1567-DET0548). Targeting / Description: Real-time URL categorisation, drive-by download blocking, typosquatting/lookalike domain alerts, SSL inspection

Coverage Details: Detecting the aftermath of a malicious web download (e.g., a browser spawning a suspicious child process like cmd.exe) is covered by our correlation rules (e.g., AN0498-T1189-DET0176). However, we have a major architectural gap regarding the network prevention layer: Real-time URL categorization, drive-by download blocking, and SSL traffic inspection are completely out of scope. A SIEM cannot actively block URLs or decrypt live SSL sessions; this physically requires an inline Secure Web Gateway (SWG) or a next-generation firewall.
Can we build it?: No. URL filtering and SSL inspection requires a proxy/gateway.

Targeting / Description: Malicious domain blocking, DNS-over-HTTPS inspection, recursive query anomaly, DNS-based exfiltration prevention
Parent Domain: Network detection & XDR correlation: Cross-source signal fusion, east-west, C2
Coverage Details: Actively blocking malicious domains (sinkholing) and preventing DNS-based exfiltration in real-time are out of scope. Furthermore, we currently have a log gap for detecting advanced DNS threats: to alert on DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) or recursive anomalies, we need dedicated DNS infrastructure telemetry (like Windows DNS Server Analytical logs or Zeek DNS logs). Once detection is closed (via missing log), response is separately solvable via SOAR playbook + Secure DNS, once integrated.
MITRE Technique: T1568.002 (DGA), T1071.004 (DNS), T1048.003 (Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol)
Can we build it?: Yes, requires DNS server logs or EDR DNS query telemetry.

Targeting / Description: Application-level micro-segmentation, device posture gate, continuous session re evaluation replacing legacy VPN
Parent Domain: Network detection & XDR correlation: Cross-source signal fusion, east-west, C2
Coverage Details: Application-level micro-segmentation, checking device posture at the gate, and continuously re-evaluating sessions are active network control capabilities. A SIEM is a passive analytics platform; it cannot act as an inline proxy to dynamically segment or block traffic. Therefore, replacing a legacy VPN with these zero-trust controls is completely out of scope and requires a dedicated ZTNA or SASE (Secure Access Service Edge) platform.
Can we build it?: No. ZTNA is an architectural enforcement mechanism, not a detection rule.

Targeting / Description: Display name spoofing, lookalike domain detection, executive impersonation alerts, vendor email compromise

Coverage Details: Detecting the endpoint aftermath of a phishing attack (e.g., a malicious Word macro executing) is covered by our correlation rules (e.g., AN0655-T1566.001-DET0236). To detect display name spoofing, lookalike domains, or executive impersonation, we absolutely need Email Gateway logs (like Proofpoint or O365 Message Trace logs). Without these specific email logs, our SIEM cannot see the phishing attempts before they reach the user.

Targeting / Description: Zero-day attachment execution in cloud sandbox, macro analysis, PDF exploit detection, password-protected archive unpacking

This capability physically requires a dedicated Email Sandbox (like Proofpoint TAP or Defender for Office 365). While we can detect the aftermath if a user actually clicks a bad attachment (via endpoint rules like AN0655-T1566.001-DET0236), the core sandboxing capability is an architectural impossibility for a SIEM.

Targeting / Description: All email links proxied through reputation engine, re-evaluated at click time to catch delayed weaponisation

Therefore, it cannot physically intercept, rewrite, or proxy email URLs. This capability requires a dedicated Secure Email Gateway (like Proofpoint TAP or Mimecast).
Can we build it?: No. Time-of-click protection is an Email Gateway feature.

Targeting / Description: Sender authentication enforcement, spoofed domain blocking, outbound policy compliance for government domain

This enforcement must happen at the Secure Email Gateway (SEG) layer (e.g., Proofpoint, O365). While we could theoretically alert on authentication failures, that is currently a log gap because we lack the email header logs to do so. Once detection is closed (via missing log), response is separately solvable via SOAR playbook + Email Gateway, once integrated.

Targeting / Description: NLP-based urgent payment request detection, anomalous bank detail change alerts, document tampering signals in attachments

This deep semantic analysis physically requires a specialized API-based email security platform (like Abnormal Security or Tessian).
Can we build it?: No. Requires ML-based email security.

Targeting / Description: Behavioural baseline per user, anomalous forwarding rule alerts, impossible travel logins, OAuth token abuse
Parent Domain: Email & collaboration security: Phishing, BEC, tender fraud, attachment threats
Coverage Details: Detecting malicious email forwarding rules created locally via PowerShell is successfully covered by rule AN1589-T1114.003-DET0576. However, we have a major log gap regarding cloud-based mailbox takeovers. To detect forwarding rules created via the Web UI, impossible travel logins, or OAuth consent abuse, we absolutely need cloud audit telemetry (specifically Office 365 Unified Audit Logs and Azure AD Audit Logs). Without these logs, our visibility into cloud mailbox compromises remains completely blind.
MITRE Technique: T1114.003 (Email Collection: Forwarding Rule), T1528 (Steal Application Access Token)
Can we build it?: Requires shifting focus from endpoint PowerShell logs to Cloud/IdP logs.

Targeting / Description: Content inspection, sensitivity label enforcement, bulk recipient alerts, classified document exfiltration blocking

Coverage Details: Actively blocking the exfiltration of classified documents and enforcing sensitivity labels on outbound emails are completely out of scope. A SIEM is a passive analytics platform; it cannot inspect email body content mid-flight or physically block an email from leaving the network. These capabilities require a dedicated Data Loss Prevention (DLP) solution (like Microsoft Purview). While we could theoretically alert on bulk external recipients, this is currently a log gap because we lack Office 365 Message Trace logs. Once detection is closed (via missing log), response is separately solvable via SOAR playbook + Email Gateway, once integrated.

Targeting / Description: AI-powered scan of structured/unstructured data, sensitivity label auto-application, PII/financial/tender document tagging

A SIEM analyzes logs of events (e.g., a record that a user opened a file); it does not crawl file systems to read the raw unstructured contents of documents. This kind of deep data discovery and classification physically requires a Data Security Posture Management (DSPM) or DLP platform (like Varonis or Microsoft Purview).
Can we build it?: Requires a dedicated product. Sigma rules could theoretically only audit the *removal* of labels.

Targeting / Description: Block/alert on sensitive data copy to USB, print, clipboard, screenshot — policy by label, content, or user group
Parent Domain: Data protection & DLP: Classification, leakage prevention, encryption
Coverage Details: Detecting basic data theft behaviors (like anomalous clipboard access or suspicious USB file copies) is covered by our correlation rules (e.g., AN0965-T1115-DET0341, AN0616-T1052.001-DET0220). However, actively blocking screenshots, restricting print jobs, or applying policies based on internal document 'content labels' are completely out of scope. A SIEM cannot physically intercept hardware actions or inspect raw file contents in real-time. These deep enforcement capabilities require a dedicated Endpoint DLP agent (like Microsoft Purview Endpoint DLP or Forcepoint).
Can we build it?: No. Blocking requires an Endpoint DLP agent.

Targeting / Description: Inspect data uploads to cloud apps, SaaS data movement policies, shadow IT detection, unsanctioned app blocking
Parent Domain: Data protection & DLP: Classification, leakage prevention, encryption
Coverage Details: Actively inspecting data uploads to cloud apps, enforcing SaaS movement policies, and blocking unsanctioned web apps are completely out of scope. A SIEM is not an inline proxy; it cannot intercept, decrypt, or block live web traffic. These capabilities physically require a dedicated Cloud Access Security Broker (CASB) or Secure Web Gateway (SWG). While we could theoretically detect 'Shadow IT' usage by analyzing network connections, this remains a log gap because we currently lack firewall traffic or DNS logs in the SIEM.

Targeting / Description: TLS 1.3 enforcement, SSL inspection, certificate pinning violation alerts, unencrypted protocol blocking

This capability physically requires a Next-Gen Firewall or Secure Web Gateway (SWG). While we do have some rules that catch the endpoint aftermath (like detecting unencrypted HTTP script downloads), the core encryption enforcement mandate of this category is an architectural impossibility.

Targeting / Description: Persistent label-based encryption that travels with the document — controls view/edit/print/forward regardless of location

Coverage Details: Applying persistent, label-based encryption that travels with a document (to control who can view, edit, or print it) is entirely out of scope. This capability physically requires a dedicated Information Rights Management (IRM) platform (like Microsoft Information Protection).

Targeting / Description: User behaviour analytics (UEBA), mass download/deletion alerts, after-hours access anomalies, resignation-pattern triggers
Parent Domain: Data protection & DLP: Classification, leakage prevention, encryption
Coverage Details: Detecting basic insider sabotage (like using command-line tools for mass file deletion or clearing event logs) is fully covered by our correlation rules (e.g., AN0411-T1485-DET0146). However, we have a significant capability gap regarding stateful User Behavior Analytics (UEBA). Sigma correlation rules are stateless queries; they cannot dynamically baseline a user's normal working hours to trigger 'after-hours anomalies' or 'resignation patterns'. Additionally, detecting mass cloud downloads is a log gap that requires Office 365 Audit logs.
Can we build it?: No. Sigma evaluates single events statelessly; it cannot do UEBA.

Targeting / Description: Cloud + on-sensor ML models for zero-day prediction, model versioned and silently updated, attack chain scoring
Parent Domain: AI security & threat intelligence: Generative AI risk, predictive detection, nation-state intel
Coverage Details: Running predictive Machine Learning (ML) models on the endpoint to score attack chains and predict zero-days is completely out of scope. Sigma rules are deterministic, logic-based queries (signatures and heuristics). They cannot train or execute AI/ML models on a host. This capability physically requires a Next-Gen Antivirus (NGAV) or an EDR agent with built-in ML sensors.
Can we build it?: No. Predictive ML is an EDR feature.

Targeting / Description: CASB-enforced block/allow/audit of ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini usage; prompt injection detection; data submitted to LLMs DLP
Parent Domain: AI security & threat intelligence: Generative AI risk, predictive detection, nation-state intel
Coverage Details: Actively blocking AI bots, inspecting data submitted to LLMs (like ChatGPT or Copilot) for DLP, and detecting prompt injections in real-time are completely out of scope. A SIEM cannot intercept web sessions to read or block chat prompts. This capability physically requires a Cloud Access Security Broker (CASB) or a dedicated GenAI Security Gateway. While we could theoretically audit AI website visits, this remains a log gap because we lack Proxy/SWG traffic logs. Once detection is closed (via missing log), response is separately solvable via SOAR playbook + SWG, once integrated.
Can we build it?: No. Requires a CASB or Secure Web Gateway.

This capability physically requires a Threat Intelligence Platform (TIP) (like ThreatConnect or MISP) integrated with a SOAR.
Can we build it?: No. Requires a TIP or SOAR.

Targeting / Description: Continuous internet-facing asset discovery, exposed credential monitoring, government domain dark web scan

This capability physically requires a dedicated External Attack Surface Management (EASM) platform (like Microsoft Defender EASM or Cortex Xpanse).

Targeting / Description: Natural language investigation, automated root cause analysis, AI-generated incident summaries, false positive suppression

Coverage Details: Using AI to automatically perform root cause analysis, suppress false positives, and generate natural language incident summaries is entirely out of scope for our correlation rules. This requires a Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response (SOAR) tool or an AI assistant (like Microsoft Security Copilot).

Coverage Details: Monitoring decoy files or 'honey-token' accounts for unauthorized access is easily achievable with our SIEM by writing custom queries for specific fake usernames or file paths. However, automatically generating, deploying, and rotating these fake credentials, decoy files, and virtual honeypot servers across the enterprise is completely out of scope. That active deployment capability physically requires a dedicated Deception Technology platform (like Thinkst Canary).
Can we build it?: No. Requires deploying actual honeypots.

Coverage Details: Proactively scanning AWS/Azure APIs to detect cloud misconfigurations, mapping assets to CIS/NIST compliance frameworks, and executing auto-remediation workflows are entirely out of scope. A SIEM analyzes logs of discrete events (e.g., a user changing a setting); it does not natively query cloud control planes to audit static configuration states. This capability physically requires a Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) platform (like Wiz or Prisma Cloud).
Can we build it?: No. Requires CSPM.

Targeting / Description: Container runtime protection, Kubernetes admission control, serverless function monitoring, cloud-native EDR agent
Parent Domain: Cloud, SaaS & OT/IoT visibility: Hybrid government infrastructure coverage
Coverage Details: Acting as a Kubernetes admission controller or providing runtime memory protection for containers is completely out of scope. A SIEM is an analytics platform; it cannot act as a cloud-native EDR agent to physically block workloads from running. This active protection physically requires a Cloud Workload Protection Platform (CWPP) agent (like Aqua or Prisma Cloud). While we could theoretically alert on malicious Docker commands, this is currently a log gap because we lack Kubernetes audit logs and container telemetry.
Can we build it?: Requires cloud-native agents deployed to workloads.

Coverage Details: Enforcing sanctioned/unsanctioned SaaS application policies and actively blocking unauthorized apps are completely out of scope. Furthermore, auditing SaaS misconfigurations (SSPM) and OAuth grants remains a severe log gap because we lack the necessary cloud API telemetry to feed into the SIEM.

Coverage Details: Performing passive, agentless discovery of IoT/OT devices (like printers or SCADA systems) and dynamically enforcing network segmentation policies are completely out of scope. Can we build it?: No. Requires NDR or OT scanner.

Parent Domain: Cloud, SaaS & OT/IoT visibility: Hybrid government infrastructure coverage
